title: Crop Steering Academy
description: Learn the root zone, understand a watering day, and practise each control before live operation.

lessons.title: Before the buttons: water, roots and air
lessons.summary: Start with the pot: roots need access to water and oxygen. A sensor describes only a small part of the root zone.
outcomes: Identify solids, water and air in the substrate.
Explain why more water is not always better.
State one limit of a local sensor reading.

slides.title: The question
body: Before you use the dashboard, identify the conditions inside the pot.
slides.narration:
Before you use the dashboard, identify the conditions inside the pot.

What do the roots need?

visual.title: The question
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Inside the root zone
body: The pot contains solid material, water, and air.
slides.narration:
The pot contains solid material, water, and air. The solid material around the roots is the substrate. Coco and stone wool are examples of substrates.

There are spaces between the solid parts. These spaces contain water or air. Roots need water and oxygen.

More water does not always improve conditions for the roots. The substrate must hold water and let excess water drain. Air must also return to some of the spaces.

visual.title: Inside the root zone
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Watch water arrive and drain
slides.narration:
Look at the spare container. Water enters the substrate. Some water stays in the substrate. Other water drains into the tray.

The amount of water then decreases. The plant uses some water. Evaporation and drainage also remove water.

A decrease in water content does not show only the water that the plant used.

visual.title: Watch water arrive and drain
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Pause before adding water
slides.narration:
This pot stays very wet. The leaves look unhealthy. Does this mean that you must add more water?

Choose one answer. Add more water immediately. Or do a check to find the cause first.

Do a check first.

Different problems can cause similar symptoms. The graph gives useful information. It does not identify every problem in the roots.

visual.title: Pause before adding water
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: What steering and sensing can do
body: Crop steering means control of conditions to influence crop growth.
slides.narration:
Crop steering means control of conditions to influence crop growth. These lessons explain irrigation. Irrigation supplies water to the crop.

The important irrigation settings control the time and quantity of each water delivery. The interval between deliveries is also important. Light, temperature, and humidity change the demand for water.

Later lessons explain vegetative steering and generative steering. These are directions of crop management. They do not guarantee a specific yield. Maximum drying is not the objective. The roots must continue to function correctly.

A sensor measures conditions at a specific location. One sensor does not measure every pot. A satisfactory reading does not prove that every dripper is clear.

Use sensor readings with equipment checks and crop observations.

The demo lets you learn the software without operation of a real pump. You do not need all the equipment to use the demo. For a new irrigation system, start with one zone.

Point to the solid material in the drawing. Point to the water. Point to the air. Give one example of information that the sensor cannot supply.

The next lesson explains volumetric water content, or VWC.

visual.title: What steering and sensing can do
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

practice.prompt: Draw an unplanted pot. Label solids, water and air. Explain why one local moisture reading cannot prove that every plant has the same conditions.
hints: Think about the spaces between solid parts.
Where is the sensing part installed?
practice.success: Pore spaces contain water or air. Roots need oxygen as well as water. A local probe cannot establish every container’s condition.

quiz.prompt: What must roots have access to?

options.text: As much water as possible.
options.feedback: More water can reduce air-filled space; it is not automatically an improvement.

options.text: Water and oxygen.
options.feedback: Both matter. Drainage and the return of air also matter.

quiz.prompt: What is substrate?

options.text: Only the nutrient solution.
options.feedback: The solution is water and dissolved material, not the whole substrate.

options.text: The growing material around the roots.
options.feedback: Coco and stone wool are examples of substrates.

quiz.prompt: A local probe shows one plausible reading. What is established?

options.text: The entire zone has healthy roots.
options.feedback: One sample cannot prove whole-zone health.

options.text: A reported value at that sensing location.
options.feedback: Other locations, freshness, calibration and physical conditions still need checking.

quiz.prompt: What does crop steering guarantee?

options.text: A specific yield if the recipe is followed.
options.feedback: A recipe does not prove the environment, water delivery or plant response.

options.text: No guaranteed crop outcome from a slider or recipe.
options.feedback: It manages conditions; suitability and outcomes need evidence.

lessons.title: VWC: what does 60% actually mean?
lessons.summary: Use equal volumes to understand volumetric water content, then separate VWC from plant-available water.
outcomes: Explain VWC as water volume divided by total measured sample volume.
Interpret 60% VWC without treating it as usable-water percentage.
Name the solids and air within the remaining volume.

slides.title: Recall before the reveal
body: The previous lesson showed three parts inside the pot.
slides.narration:
The previous lesson showed three parts inside the pot.

Name these parts before the answer appears.

visual.title: Recall before the reveal
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Six out of ten
body: The three parts are solid material, water, and air.
slides.narration:
The three parts are solid material, water, and air.

VWC means volumetric water content. It is the volume of water divided by the total volume of the sample. The result is usually a percentage.

The drawing divides a sample into ten equal volumes. Water occupies six of these volumes. Six divided by ten is zero point six. Multiply this result by one hundred to get sixty percent.

This example has sixty percent VWC. The blocks explain the volume ratio. In a real substrate, water occupies spaces between solid parts. It does not form the separate blocks in this drawing.

visual.title: Six out of ten
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Put litres beside the fraction
body: This example uses a representative sample with a total volume of five liters.
slides.narration:
This example uses a representative sample with a total volume of five liters. Its VWC is sixty percent. Five multiplied by zero point six is three. Thus, the sample contains three liters of water.

This calculation explains the amount of water already in the sample. It is not an instruction to add three liters to a five-liter pot.

visual.title: Put litres beside the fraction
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: The probe sees a region
body: Sixty percent of the total volume is water.
slides.narration:
Sixty percent of the total volume is water. Is all the remaining forty percent air?

No. The remaining volume includes solid material and air. VWC alone does not give the complete air volume.

Sixty percent VWC does not mean that sixty percent of the water available to the plant remains. Some water stays more tightly attached to the substrate. Different substrates hold water differently. VWC alone does not show the time until the plant needs water.

Look at the probe location. The probe measures a local region. Its installation, contact, calibration, and location affect the reading.

A probe near one dripper might not represent a dry pot at the end of a row. Later lessons explain how to select locations that represent the zone.

visual.title: The probe sees a region
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Teach it back
body: The sensor now shows forty percent VWC.
slides.narration:
The sensor now shows forty percent VWC. Does this reading always mean that the substrate is too dry?

No. The reading alone is not sufficient. You also need information about the substrate, validated reference values, crop, and conditions. One VWC target is not correct for every system.

Do not select a target yet. Complete this sentence. Sixty percent VWC means what?

Approximately sixty percent of the measured sample volume is water. This is one correct answer.

The reading does not give the exact water volume available to the plant. One sensor does not prove that all pots have the same conditions.

Use these limits when you assess advice about VWC.

The next lesson explains why a full pot does not mean one hundred percent VWC.

visual.title: Teach it back
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

practice.prompt: Imagine ten equal total substrate volumes. Four contain water. What is VWC? What else may occupy the remaining six?
hints: Water volume ÷ total sample volume × 100.
Recall solids and pore spaces from A1.
practice.success: 40% VWC. The remainder includes solids and air; it is not automatically 60% air or 60% usable water.

quiz.prompt: Three of ten equal sample volumes contain water. What is VWC?

options.feedback: 70% is the remainder, not the water fraction.

quiz.prompt: Does 60% VWC mean 60% of usable water remains?

options.text: Yes, it is a fuel gauge for the plant.
options.feedback: That interpretation confuses measured water content with plant-available water.

options.text: No. It describes water volume in the measured sample.
options.feedback: Plant availability depends on more than that volume fraction.

quiz.prompt: At 60% VWC, is the remaining 40% all air?

options.text: Yes. Water and air are the only components.
options.feedback: Recall the solid growing material introduced in A1.

options.text: No. The remainder also includes solid material.
options.feedback: Total substrate volume includes solids, water and air.

quiz.prompt: How do you interpret a changing VWC line?

options.text: Treat the change as litres consumed by all plants.
options.feedback: A local volume fraction is not a zone water meter or uptake measurement.

options.text: Check the identified probe, units, time and context.
options.feedback: The line describes sampled water content; evidence still matters.

instructions: Imagine ten equal total substrate volumes. Four contain water. What is VWC? What else may occupy the remaining six?
Explain your reasoning to another person or record a short teach-back.

lessons.title: When is a pot full? Capacity versus saturation
lessons.summary: Separate saturation, a documented drained container condition, and the program’s configured field-capacity reference.
outcomes: Distinguish saturation from drained container capacity.
Explain why the app reference is not a physical capacity measurement.
Describe conditions that must be documented during a capacity check.

slides.title: What does full mean?
body: A grower asks for a full pot.
slides.narration:
A grower asks for a full pot. What does full mean?

VWC is water volume divided by total sample volume. The total sample volume also includes solid material. A correctly irrigated pot does not need a reading of one hundred percent VWC.

visual.title: What does full mean?
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Saturation is a physical state
slides.narration:
Saturation is one physical condition. At saturation, water fills the pore spaces. Pore spaces are the spaces between solid parts of the substrate. The solid material remains present.

Continuous saturation around the roots is not the objective.

visual.title: Saturation is a physical state
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Observe drainage
body: Water drains from the spare pot into the tray.
slides.narration:
Water drains from the spare pot into the tray. After a specified drainage procedure, some water remains in the substrate. Some spaces contain air again.

The retained water quantity depends on the substrate and container conditions. Container height is one of these conditions. Container capacity describes the retained water under specified container and drainage conditions.

Growers sometimes call their reference value field capacity. The program also uses this term. Field capacity originally describes a condition in field soil. A pot or substrate block has different physical conditions.

Identify the drainage method that applies to the reference value.

One drainage time is not correct for all pots. Use a documented method suitable for the substrate and system. Record the container type. Record the substrate type. Record the initial condition. Record the drainage interval.

Record the probe installation. Do the procedure again. If the results change, find the cause before you use the reference value.

Container weight and visible drainage give additional information during the procedure. A suitable sensor gives another measurement. These measurements do not correct poor probe contact or a location that does not represent the zone.

visual.title: Observe drainage
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Physical state or entered setting?
body: The dashboard contains a reference setting.
slides.narration:
The dashboard contains a reference setting. A person entered this value into the program. The displayed value does not prove that the measurement procedure was correct.

Keep a measured physical condition separate from a software setting.

visual.title: Physical state or entered setting?
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: An example is not your target
body: The example reference value is sixty percent.
slides.narration:
The example reference value is sixty percent. Must your substrate use the same reference value?

No. Sixty percent is only the example value. Your reference value needs measurement evidence for your substrate and container. The measurement method must also be suitable.

The highest sensor reading is not automatically the correct reference value. A temporary peak does not prove correct calibration. Poor contact or an incorrect reading does not establish a reference value.

There are three cards in this exercise. The first card is saturation. The second card is drained container capacity. The third card is the reference setting in the program.

Identify the cards that describe physical conditions. Identify the card that describes a software setting.

Saturation and drained container capacity describe physical conditions. The configured reference is a software setting. A useful setting represents a suitable measured condition. A value without measurement evidence is not sufficient.

The next lesson explains dryback. Dryback is a decrease in substrate water content between irrigation events. A decrease of fifteen percentage points is different from fifteen percent relative dryback.

visual.title: An example is not your target
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

practice.prompt: Label three cards: all pore spaces filled with water; water retained after a specified drainage procedure; a number entered in the app. Which card proves a measured container condition?
hints: A setting is not a measurement.
Document medium, container, probe and drainage method.
practice.success: The cards describe saturation, a drained container condition and a configured reference. Only a suitably documented measurement supports the actual container condition.

quiz.prompt: What does saturation describe?

options.text: Every probe must display 100% VWC.
options.feedback: Solids remain part of total sample volume, and measurement methods have limits.

options.text: Water fills the pore spaces.
options.feedback: It is a physical condition, distinct from the drained state.

quiz.prompt: What establishes a useful drained reference?

options.text: The highest number ever seen on the graph.
options.feedback: A peak can reflect different conditions or faulty evidence.

options.text: A documented, repeatable check under specified conditions.
options.feedback: Record the substrate, container, probe, procedure and drainage conditions.

quiz.prompt: The app field-capacity value is set to 60%. What is proven?

options.text: Every container holds 60% after drainage.
options.feedback: Different containers, media, probes and procedures can produce different measurements.

options.text: Only that the reference is configured to 60%.
options.feedback: A configuration value alone does not establish physical container capacity.

quiz.prompt: Can a demonstration pot define every live zone’s target?

options.text: Yes, if the picture looks similar.
options.feedback: Appearance alone does not establish comparable substrate and drainage conditions.

options.text: No. Suitability requires local evidence.
options.feedback: The spare-pot demonstration teaches concepts, not a universal recipe.

instructions: Label three cards: all pore spaces filled with water; water retained after a specified drainage procedure; a number entered in the app. Which card proves a measured container condition?
Explain your reasoning to another person or record a short teach-back.

lessons.title: Dryback without the confusing maths
lessons.summary: Describe a water-content drop in percentage points and as a percentage of its starting value.
outcomes: Calculate a VWC drop in percentage points.
Calculate relative dryback from a stated starting value.
Check the convention before interpreting a dryback field.

slides.title: One drop, two descriptions
body: VWC is water volume divided by measured sample volume.
Dryback is a fall in water content over an interval.
slides.narration: Recall the ten equal volumes from lesson A2. VWC describes how much of the measured sample volume is water. It does not say how much usable water remains. Now compare two readings from the same probe. A fall in water content over an interval is called dryback. We can describe that fall in two ways. First name the starting and ending readings, then state which calculation you used.

visual.title: One drop, two descriptions
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Subtract to get percentage points
slides.narration: Our teaching sample starts at sixty percent VWC and ends at forty-five percent. Subtract forty-five from sixty. The drop is fifteen percentage points. A percentage point is the difference between two percentage readings. We have not yet calculated a relative percentage. Keep both timestamps with the readings. This example explains arithmetic. It does not establish a suitable dryback for a crop, a container, or a medium.

visual.title: Subtract to get percentage points
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Describe a fall from 60% to 45% VWC.
steps: Subtract: 60 - 45 = 15 percentage points.
Divide the drop by the starting value: 15 / 60 = 0.25.
Multiply by 100: relative dryback = 25%.

slides.title: Divide to get relative dryback
slides.narration: For relative dryback, ask what fraction of the starting reading was lost. Divide the fifteen-point drop by the starting value of sixty. The result is one quarter. Multiply by one hundred to express it as a percentage. That gives twenty-five percent relative dryback. The denominator means the number you divide by. Use the starting reading. Using the ending reading answers a different question. A zero starting value cannot be used in this division.

visual.title: Divide to get relative dryback
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Pause and complete the steps
slides.narration: Pause and complete this partly filled example. The start is eighty percent and the end is sixty percent. Eighty minus sixty gives a drop of how many points? Put that same drop over eighty, then multiply by one hundred. Resume when you have both labels. The answers are twenty percentage points and twenty-five percent relative dryback. Notice that the relative result matches the previous example, although the point drop differs.

visual.title: Pause and complete the steps
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Try new numbers without the steps
body: Report both answers with their labels.
slides.narration: Now work independently. A fresh record starts at fifty percent VWC and ends at forty percent. Write both descriptions before you continue. The point drop is ten. Ten divided by fifty, times one hundred, gives twenty percent relative dryback. Saying only ten percent dryback would hide your convention. When you hand over a record, include the two VWC readings, the interval, the calculation, and the result with its label.

visual.title: Try new numbers without the steps
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Read a program field carefully
slides.narration: The planner guide defines morning dryback relative to a peak. Suppose its peak is sixty percent and the example field says ten percent relative dryback. Ten percent of sixty is six. Subtract six from sixty to get a fifty-four percent VWC reference. Do not subtract ten points unless a field explicitly uses points. Read the help for the actual field. A configured reference describes a rule; it does not prove the crop reached it.

visual.title: Read a program field carefully
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Check meaning before making a claim
body: Water loss is not a measurement of plant uptake.
slides.narration: Finish by recalling A3. A configured reference is different from a measured physical condition. The same distinction applies here. A calculated dryback describes two observations only when their units, probe identity, and timestamps are trustworthy. Water can leave the measured region through drainage and evaporation as well as plant use. This calculation does not separate those paths. Tomorrow, explain the difference between points and relative percentage aloud, using numbers you choose yourself.

visual.title: Check meaning before making a claim
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

practice.prompt: Calculate both dryback descriptions for 70% to 56% VWC. Then find the VWC reference for 10% relative dryback from a 50% peak.
hints: Subtract the end from the start.
Divide the drop by the start for relative dryback.
practice.success: 14 percentage points; 20% relative dryback; 45% VWC reference. Explain each denominator.

quiz.prompt: A reading falls from 50% to 40% VWC. Which description is correct?

options.text: 10 percentage points and 20% relative dryback
options.feedback: The drop is 10 points; 10 / 50 × 100 is 20%.

options.text: 10 percentage points and 10% relative dryback
options.feedback: Ten is the point difference. The relative result uses 50 as the denominator and is 20%.

options.text: 20 percentage points and 10% relative dryback
options.feedback: Subtract first: 50 - 40 is 10 points. Dividing 10 by 50 gives 20%.

quiz.prompt: A 60% peak loses 10% of its starting value. What is the resulting VWC?

options.feedback: That subtracts 10 percentage points. A relative loss is 10% of 60, which is 6 points.
The loss is 6 points, so 60 - 6 = 54% VWC.
Six is the point loss. Subtract it from the starting reading to obtain the ending VWC.

quiz.prompt: Why is the note “15% dryback” incomplete?

options.text: It needs a higher target.
options.feedback: The problem is missing meaning, not target size. State points or relative percentage and the interval.

options.text: It does not state the calculation convention.
options.feedback: Fifteen points and 15% of a starting value usually give different ending readings.

options.text: Dryback can only be expressed in points.
options.feedback: Both points and relative percentage are useful when clearly labelled.

quiz.prompt: What does a 60% VWC reading establish?

options.text: Exactly 60% of usable water remains.
options.feedback: VWC is water volume divided by total measured sample volume. Availability is a different property.

options.text: Every pot has the same water content.
options.feedback: A probe samples a local region. Other pots may differ.

options.text: About 60% of the measured sample volume is water.
options.feedback: That is the VWC definition from A2; it does not establish availability or zone uniformity.

instructions: On paper, explain 60% to 45% using both conventions.
Repeat with 50% to 40%, then check your answers.
Use no live irrigation settings for this exercise.

lessons.title: EC: what it measures, and which EC you are looking at
lessons.summary: Identify feed, bulk, pore-water and runoff EC before comparing readings.
outcomes: Define EC without calling it an individual nutrient analysis.
Label four EC types by sample location or method.
Explain why bulk EC cannot simply be renamed pore-water EC.

slides.title: A number needs a measurement label
body: Electrical conductivity is shortened to EC.
EC reflects how readily an electrical current passes.
slides.narration: A meter shows a number beside EC. EC means electrical conductivity. It describes how readily an electrical current passes through the measured material. Dissolved charged particles, called ions, influence conductivity. The number does not identify each nutrient. Before interpreting it, find the measurement type, unit, whether the meter adjusts for temperature, and the sample method. Recall A2: a familiar percentage can hide a wrong meaning. An EC number also needs its full label.

visual.title: A number needs a measurement label
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Follow the sample locations
body: Runoff/extract: collected by a stated procedure.
slides.narration: Follow four labelled places. Feed EC comes from the solution supplied to the plants. Bulk EC describes the combined medium around a probe. Pore-water EC describes the water within the spaces in that medium. Runoff or extract EC describes a collected sample made by a stated procedure. Collection methods matter. A drainage cup and a laboratory extract are not interchangeable simply because both contain water from the root region.

visual.title: Follow the sample locations
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Worked example: label before comparing
body: TEROS 12 direct EC output: bulk EC.
Keep the labels even when numbers match.
slides.narration: Here is a worked record. A tank sample measures two point zero millisiemens per centimetre. Label that value feed EC. A TEROS twelve probe reports zero point eight in the same unit from the medium. Label its direct conductivity output bulk EC. The unequal numbers alone do not prove an error. We measured different things. Copy the sample location and method into each record before you consider a comparison.

visual.title: Worked example: label before comparing
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Label a tank reading of 2.0 mS/cm and a TEROS 12 direct conductivity reading of 0.8 mS/cm.
steps: Find where each sample or measurement came from.
Label the supplied solution feed EC.
Label the direct TEROS 12 conductivity output bulk EC.
workedExample.answer: Feed EC 2.0 mS/cm; bulk EC 0.8 mS/cm. The difference alone does not diagnose nutrition.

slides.title: A conversion needs evidence
body: Check its required inputs and valid range.
slides.narration: A display may calculate pore-water EC from other measurements. That calculation is a model, with assumptions and a valid operating range. Check the documented method and its required inputs. A label change is not a conversion. Do not compare a feed reference with a bulk reading as if they were the same measurement. Ask the installer what the displayed reading represents. Keep an unknown type marked unknown until its origin is established.

visual.title: A conversion needs evidence
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Pause and finish the labels
body: Water collected by a drainage protocol: __.
Water in pores, using an identified method: __.
slides.narration: Complete this partly labelled diagram. The supplied solution is already labelled feed EC. What label belongs to a cup collected using a documented drainage procedure? What label belongs to water within the medium, measured or estimated by an identified suitable method? Pause first. The answers are runoff EC and pore-water EC. Keep the collection procedure with the runoff result. These labels describe evidence. They do not prescribe a target to copy.

visual.title: Pause and finish the labels
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Try a new record independently
body: Label both and name what the record cannot establish.
slides.narration: Now try a new record independently. The supply sample reads one point seven millisiemens per centimetre. A drainage cup reads two point four. Label both readings and state what else you need before interpreting the difference. Check collection timing, method, meter checks, and whether the meter adjusts for temperature. This pair cannot identify an excessive individual nutrient. It also cannot establish the pore-water EC throughout every pot. Different media and methods need locally justified interpretation.

visual.title: Try a new record independently
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Use EC with the rest of the record
body: No universal substrate EC target is taught here.
Compare like measurement types and methods.
slides.narration: Recall dryback from A4. A correct calculation still needs trustworthy readings and a stated interval. Use that same discipline with EC. Write the type beside every value, compare like methods, and retain the crop and substrate context. This course gives no universal substrate EC target. A surprising number starts an investigation. It does not justify adding fertiliser, flushing a crop, or changing a protection without the responsible operator and supporting evidence.

visual.title: Use EC with the rest of the record
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

practice.prompt: Label these new samples: supply solution at 1.9 mS/cm; direct TEROS 12 output at 0.6 mS/cm; water extracted by a stated laboratory procedure at 2.7 mS/cm. Explain why these numbers cannot identify an individual deficient nutrient.
hints: Start with sample location, not number size.
An extract result keeps its extraction method.
practice.success: Feed EC; bulk EC; extract EC. EC gives conductivity information, not the concentration of each nutrient.

quiz.prompt: A TEROS 12 provides a direct conductivity measurement in the medium. What type is it?

options.text: Feed EC
options.feedback: Feed EC measures supplied solution. The direct TEROS 12 measurement is bulk EC.

options.text: Bulk EC
options.feedback: The direct conductivity output describes the bulk medium. A pore-water estimate needs an identified conversion.

options.text: Automatically pore-water EC
options.feedback: A bulk measurement is not automatically pore-water EC. Check the conversion and its valid range.

quiz.prompt: Two readings have the same unit but different sample methods. What should you do first?

options.text: Compare them directly because the units match.
options.feedback: Matching units do not make feed, bulk, pore-water and extract values interchangeable.

options.text: Change the lower value to match the higher one.
options.feedback: A difference may reflect measurement type. Establish type and method before making an operational decision.

options.text: Identify both measurement types and methods.
options.feedback: This establishes what the numbers represent and whether a comparison is meaningful.

quiz.prompt: A high EC reading alone tells you which of these?

options.text: Exactly which nutrient is excessive.
options.feedback: EC does not separate individual ions into a nutrient analysis.

options.text: The conductivity under the measurement conditions.
options.feedback: Interpret it with type, method, temperature treatment and crop context.

options.text: A universal target has been exceeded.
options.feedback: Suitable interpretation depends on crop, medium and measurement method. This lesson supplies no universal target.

quiz.prompt: A value labelled pore-water EC was calculated from bulk EC. What must accompany it?

options.text: Only a new display name.
options.feedback: Renaming the entity does not establish a valid conversion.

options.text: The assumption that all EC types are equal.
options.feedback: The methods are related but measure different things.

options.text: An identified conversion method, inputs and validity limits.
options.feedback: A model needs its assumptions and operating range documented before interpretation.

instructions: Draw the feed-to-container-to-drain path on paper.
Add all four EC labels, including bulk and pore-water within the container.
Explain one conclusion an EC number alone cannot support.

lessons.title: Can you trust that reading?
lessons.summary: Check identity, freshness, units, placement and calibration before interpreting a trace.
outcomes: Identify stale data even when its line looks smooth.
Build a short sensor-check record.
Choose a safe investigation before changing targets.

slides.title: A smooth line can be old
body: Read the timestamp, not only the line.
slides.narration: A graph looks steady. Does that mean the root region is steady? First check when the last valid observation arrived. Freshness means the information is recent enough for the decision. A browser can keep showing an old value. A flat line can also be a real steady reading. Its shape alone cannot decide between those cases. Recall A5: first establish what a number measures. Now add when and where it was measured.

visual.title: A smooth line can be old
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Worked example: calculate the age
body: Age: four hours. Another probe changed at 13:59.
slides.narration: Work through a synthetic record. The clock says fourteen hundred. Probe A last supplied a valid observation at ten hundred. Its data are four hours old. Probe B in another representative location updated at thirteen fifty-nine. The difference raises a sensing question before a crop-response question. Record both identities and ages. Check availability, communication and power through the approved procedure. Do not turn an old reading into a watering instruction.

visual.title: Worked example: calculate the age
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: At 14:00, probe A last updated at 10:00. What is the first finding?
steps: Confirm the timestamp belongs to the last valid observation.
Subtract 10:00 from 14:00.
Record four-hour-old data and investigate its source.
workedExample.answer: Probe A has four-hour-old data. The record cannot establish current water content.

slides.title: Match identity and units
body: Check the real zone and probe label.
slides.narration: Next match the room, zone and probe to the physical label. Similar names are not proof. Then read the unit. A VWC value of zero point four five cubic metres per cubic metre equals forty-five percent. Treating zero point four five as zero point four five percent creates a hundredfold scale error. For EC, retain the measurement type from A5. Read the original reading and displayed reading together when tracing a mismatch.

visual.title: Match identity and units
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Check what the probe represents
body: Calibration relates the signal to water content.
Use the documented method for that sensor and medium.
slides.narration: Calibration is the method that relates the sensor signal to the reported quantity. Confirm that the documented calibration suits the medium. Check installation records and physical placement with the responsible person. Poor contact or an air gap can distort a moisture reading. A probe beside one emitter may not represent another part of the container. Agreement between probes helps, but two probes can share the same error. Do not average away an unexplained disagreement.

visual.title: Check what the probe represents
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Pause and finish the check
body: Identity and units checked; next check = __.
slides.narration: Complete this partly finished check. It is fifteen thirty. The last valid observation was fifteen twenty-five. How old is it? Identity and units already match. Name another check before accepting the whole zone as represented. Pause now. The age is five minutes. Next checks can include suitable placement, calibration records, and comparison with independent evidence. Five minutes describes age only. It is not a universal guarantee that any control decision is safe.

visual.title: Pause and finish the check
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Try a changed scenario independently
slides.narration: Work independently on changed numbers. At sixteen twenty, one display still shows forty-eight percent from twelve twenty. Another representative probe reports forty-three percent at sixteen nineteen. State the age of each result. Then write three checks in order. Start with identity and last valid observations. Check availability and the communication path. Follow with a suitable physical or independent check. Do not conclude that every pot is dry from either single number.

visual.title: Try a changed scenario independently
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Restore evidence before changing targets
body: Record the fault and follow the local fallback procedure.
Do not bypass a protection to make a shot happen.
slides.narration: Recall A3: the configured capacity reference is not proof of physical capacity. Likewise, a plausible display is not proof of valid sensing. Independent evidence may include a documented reference measurement and a competent physical inspection appropriate to the installation. If sensing is unreliable, follow the local safe fallback procedure and involve the responsible operator. Do not lower a protection to force watering. Your exercise ends with a reasoned check record, without changing live equipment.

visual.title: Restore evidence before changing targets
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

practice.prompt: At 09:45, probe A last reported 55% at 06:45. Probe B reports 50% at 09:44. Explain what is known, what remains unknown and your first three checks.
hints: Compute ages before judging values.
Disagreement may involve identity, communication, placement or calibration.
practice.success: A is three hours old; B is one minute old. Current zone uniformity is unknown. Verify identity/timestamps, availability/communications, then suitable physical and calibration evidence.

quiz.prompt: At 11:00, the last valid observation is from 07:30. What do you know?

options.text: The current VWC is proven by the display.
options.feedback: The display contains an observation from 3 hours 30 minutes ago. Current VWC remains unknown.

options.text: The observation is 3 hours 30 minutes old.
options.feedback: Subtract the timestamps. Check freshness and source before interpreting current crop conditions.

options.text: The crop has stopped using water.
options.feedback: An old or flat trace cannot establish plant water use.

quiz.prompt: Two probes agree. What does their agreement prove?

options.text: The whole zone is uniform.
options.feedback: Two local samples do not prove every container or location is the same.

options.text: Calibration must be correct.
options.feedback: Both probes may share a calibration or placement error.

options.text: Their reported values agree; other checks are still needed.
options.feedback: Agreement is useful evidence, alongside identity, freshness, calibration and placement.

quiz.prompt: An unreliable probe is holding irrigation. What is the next response?

options.text: Lower a protection to force a shot.
options.feedback: That bypasses the fault instead of restoring trustworthy evidence. Follow the safe fallback procedure.

options.text: Investigate sensing and follow the local safe fallback procedure.
options.feedback: Resolve identity, freshness, communication and physical evidence with the responsible operator.

options.text: Treat the old number as a current measurement.
options.feedback: An old value does not establish the current condition.

quiz.prompt: The source reports 0.45 m³/m³ VWC. Which percentage matches it?

options.feedback: A volume fraction of 0.45 becomes 45% when multiplied by 100.
The fraction and percentage express the same water-to-sample volume ratio.
That is a scale error. Multiply 0.45 by 100 to obtain 45%.

lessons.title: Read water and EC on the same graph
lessons.summary: Read both axes, find day and night, and keep recorded evidence separate from a planning reference.
outcomes: Locate time, VWC and EC axes on a combined chart.
Identify shots, the night period and missing or stale evidence.
Explain why a draft reference can move while recorded data remain unchanged.

slides.title: Start with time
body: This graph shows water content and EC over time.
slides.narration:
This graph shows water content and EC over time. We will examine one part at a time.

Time is on the bottom axis. Later times are farther to the right. The shaded area shows the night period in this example. Night shading does not mean that the sensor stopped measurement.

visual.title: Start with time
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Add water content
slides.narration:
The first line shows VWC. Read this line against the percentage scale on the left.

This point shows sixty percent VWC at the indicated time. The solid line connects the example observations.

In a live system, do a check of the reading age. Identify gaps in the readings.

visual.title: Add water content
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Add EC and a second scale
slides.narration:
EC means electrical conductivity. The EC line uses the scale on the right. The unit is millisiemens per centimeter.

Identify the EC measurement assigned to the graph.

Feed EC, bulk substrate EC, and pore-water EC describe different measurements. These names are not interchangeable.

The VWC line and EC line cross on the screen. Does this mean that the measured values are equal?

No. VWC and EC have different units and scales. Each line shows how its measurement changes with time.

Do not subtract a VWC value from an EC value.

visual.title: Add EC and a second scale
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Events, observations and references
slides.narration:
The markers show irrigation events. Water content can increase after water reaches the probe. Water content then decreases between events.

EC also changes. The EC line does not need to be the opposite shape of the VWC line. Water delivery, mixing, drainage, temperature, measurement method, and crop conditions affect the readings. One line does not prove the cause of a change.

The graph also shows a planning reference. The program draws this reference from the selected settings. A measured line shows observations. A planning reference shows the behavior illustrated by the software. These lines need different labels, even when their positions are the same.

visual.title: Events, observations and references
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Continue into night; move a threshold
body: The planning reference continues through the night to the next morning.
slides.narration:
The planning reference continues through the night to the next morning. An unexplained break makes the reference difficult to read. A continuous line does not prove a correct prediction of the crop response.

The overnight EC reference connects the last daytime reference to the next morning reference. This connection is not a separately scheduled P3 EC target. It does not calculate or prove the behavior of salts overnight.

Now watch this demo edit. We increase the P3 emergency VWC threshold in the local draft. The draft threshold changes from thirty-five percent to thirty-nine percent. The saved threshold remains visible for comparison. The measured example readings remain the same.

visual.title: Continue into night; move a threshold
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Explain what changed
body: A draft, not a guaranteed shot
slides.narration:
Which item changed? The previous water content? The local draft of a threshold? Or a guaranteed irrigation event?

The local draft of the threshold changed. Review and application of the settings are separate actions. The controller uses its conditions and protection rules to decide if irrigation occurs. The emergency threshold is not a normal overnight target.

Point to the time axis. Point to the VWC scale. Point to the EC scale. Identify one irrigation marker. Identify one planning reference. Find the reading age.

The next lesson explains the irrigation phases from P0 to P3.

visual.title: Explain what changed
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

practice.prompt: Open the practice graph. Move the example emergency VWC threshold from 35% to 39%. Which line changes? Can this edit change yesterday’s recorded moisture?
hints: A proposal and a measurement are different evidence types.
The emergency threshold is protective, not a routine overnight goal.
practice.success: The draft threshold moves. The fixed synthetic actual trace does not move. A reference edit cannot rewrite measured history.

quiz.prompt: Which axis belongs to VWC on the teaching chart?

options.text: The right EC axis because both lines overlap.
options.feedback: Line crossings do not make their units equivalent.

options.text: The left axis, in percent.
options.feedback: The EC line has its own right-hand conductivity axis.

quiz.prompt: A draft threshold moves. What happens to recorded history?

options.text: The recorded VWC curve moves to match.
options.feedback: Changing a target cannot rewrite sensor measurements.

options.text: It stays unchanged.
options.feedback: A draft is a proposed setting; recorded evidence is separate.

quiz.prompt: A smooth flat trace has an old timestamp. What next?

options.text: Assume the crop is perfectly stable.
options.feedback: Appearance is not proof that readings are current.

options.text: Investigate freshness and identity before acting on it.
options.feedback: A convincing line can still be stale.

quiz.prompt: What does the overnight EC planning connection prove?

options.text: That the program actively holds a scheduled P3 EC target.
options.feedback: The illustrative line is not proof of an independent EC control loop.

options.text: Only a reference connection between illustrated endpoints.
options.feedback: There is no independent scheduled P3 EC target or guaranteed EC forecast.

Explain your reasoning to another person or record a short teach-back.

lessons.title: P0 to P3: build the day one phase at a time
lessons.summary: Explain the program’s four phases and separate a projected timetable from actual decisions.
outcomes: Name the four program phases and their purposes.
Explain why projected shot times are conditional.
Distinguish an overnight emergency floor from an ordinary target.

slides.title: A phase is part of a control sequence
slides.narration: A phase is one part of the program sequence, with its own purpose and rules. This program names four phases: P zero, morning dryback; P one, ramp-up; P two, maintenance; and P three, overnight. Those names belong to this program. Recall B1: time belongs on the horizontal axis, and actual readings differ from reference lines. A phase label helps explain the rule in use. It does not prove that water flowed.

visual.title: A phase is part of a control sequence
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: P0: begin with morning dryback
body: The grow-day begins at configured lights-on.
P0 uses dryback and timing rules.
slides.narration: At configured lights-on, the program begins a new grow-day in P zero. Morning dryback allows water content to fall before the ramp begins. Recall A4: a relative dryback uses the peak as its denominator. The program also has timing rules, including a maximum wait. Do not assume the first shot must occur at a fixed clock time. Read the reported phase and reason, and confirm the lighting schedule against the actual installation.

visual.title: P0: begin with morning dryback
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: P1: build water content with shots
body: A shot is one watering event.
Ramp-up uses repeated shots and checks.
slides.narration: A shot is one watering event. P one uses shots to build water content toward the configured peak target. The program checks conditions between events and applies its limits. A target is a reference used by a rule, not a promise of the next probe value. The real response depends on delivery, drainage and the sampled region. Do not infer the number of completed shots merely from the steps drawn on a planning curve.

visual.title: P1: build water content with shots
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: P2: maintain with conditional events
body: Projected events are not booked appointments.
slides.narration: P two is maintenance. A re-water threshold is a reference used when deciding whether another shot is needed. Conditions and protections still matter. A planning chart may draw several evenly spaced events using an assumed drying rate. The actual controller responds to its rules and readings. A slower decline can mean fewer events than the chart shows. Check recent sensor data and the next-action explanation before you interpret a missing shot as a fault.

visual.title: P2: maintain with conditional events
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Worked example: explain the sequence
body: Exact P1/P2 transition times are not supplied.
slides.narration: Work through a fictional lighting day from six in the morning to six in the evening. Start with P zero at lights-on. Explain the morning dryback, then P one ramp-up, then P two maintenance. P three covers the overnight period; the rules can end daytime watering before lights-off. We cannot calculate exact transition times from the lighting hours alone. Record the displayed reason and actual observations instead of treating the illustration as a timetable.

visual.title: Worked example: explain the sequence
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Explain a 06:00–18:00 lighting day without inventing shot times.
steps: Place P0 at the start of the grow-day.
Describe P1 ramp-up and P2 maintenance by purpose.
Describe P3 overnight and its separate emergency floor.
workedExample.answer: The sequence explains rules and purposes. Lighting hours alone do not determine exact transitions or shot counts.

slides.title: P3: keep the emergency floor separate
body: The emergency floor is a protection reference.
It is not an ordinary destination to chase.
slides.narration: P three covers overnight dryback. Its emergency floor is a separate protection reference, used by the overnight rescue rule when its conditions permit. It is not an ordinary target that the operator should try to reach every night. Recall A6: if a reading is unreliable, investigate and follow the local fallback procedure. A low or old number is not permission to bypass a hold. The physical system still needs the approved handover and protections.

visual.title: P3: keep the emergency floor separate
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Complete, then explain a new day
body: Complete: P0 __; P1 ramp-up; P2 __; P3 overnight.
slides.narration: Pause and complete the two missing phase purposes: P zero is what, and P two is what? They are morning dryback and maintenance. Now independently explain a different lighting day, from eight in the morning to eight in the evening. Put the four phase cards in order. State which exact shot times remain unknown. Explain why moving the emergency floor would change a rule reference without rewriting the measured water-content trace.

visual.title: Complete, then explain a new day
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

practice.prompt: For a fictional 07:00–19:00 lighting day, order all four phase cards and explain one purpose per card. Explain why a chart with six P2 events does not promise six actual events.
hints: Use P0 morning dryback, P1 ramp-up, P2 maintenance and P3 overnight.
A projection uses assumptions; events still depend on rules and observations.
practice.success: Correct order and purposes; conditional events and protections prevent a guaranteed count. The P3 floor is an emergency reference, not a routine destination.

quiz.prompt: Which order matches this program’s normal day sequence?

options.text: P0 morning dryback → P1 ramp-up → P2 maintenance → P3 overnight
options.feedback: These are the four phases in order. Actual transitions also depend on conditions and timing rules.

options.text: P0 overnight → P1 maintenance → P2 ramp-up → P3 morning
options.feedback: The labels are reversed. P0 is morning dryback; P3 is overnight.
Begin at lights-on with P0, then ramp-up, maintenance and overnight.

quiz.prompt: A planning curve shows P2 shots at exact times. What do those times establish?

options.text: Guaranteed pump appointments.
options.feedback: The projection uses a drying rate. Actual events depend on rules, fresh readings and protections.

options.text: Illustrative times under the projection’s assumptions.
options.feedback: Use actual event records to determine what happened.

options.text: Proof those shots already completed.
options.feedback: Actual event and delivery evidence are needed to support a claim about completed watering.

quiz.prompt: What is the P3 emergency floor?

options.text: A routine nightly destination to chase.
options.feedback: It is a separate protection reference, not a routine moisture target.

options.text: Proof that a rescue shot must always occur.
options.feedback: The rescue rule still has conditions and protections. A threshold does not guarantee a shot.

options.text: A reference used by the overnight rescue rule.
options.feedback: Keep its protection role separate from ordinary targets and projected dryback.

quiz.prompt: What can configured lights-on and lights-off times alone tell you?

options.text: Every P1 shot time.
options.feedback: Ramp timing also depends on configured rules and observed conditions.

options.text: The lighting period used as context for the grow-day.
options.feedback: Verify it matches the actual installation; it does not fully determine irrigation transitions.

options.text: The exact amount each plant takes up.
options.feedback: Lighting hours do not measure delivery or uptake.

instructions: Draw a blank day strip using fictional lighting hours.
Place the four phase cards and write their purposes.
Label assumed event times projected; label recorded events actual.

lessons.title: Vegetative and generative: a bias, not a magic switch
lessons.summary: Understand steering direction and how the planner blends operator-defined endpoints.
outcomes: Separate steering direction from growth stage.
Calculate a simple blend between configured endpoints.
Explain why pot size alone cannot establish safe recipe values.

slides.title: Name a direction before a setting
body: Vegetative growth includes roots, leaves and shoots.
Generative growth includes flowers and fruit.
Bias means the intended management direction.
slides.narration: Vegetative growth includes roots, leaves and shoots. Generative growth includes reproductive structures, such as flowers and fruit. A steering bias is a management direction intended to influence growth. It is not a guarantee of a plant response. A flowering crop can still receive a vegetative bias for a particular purpose. Recall B2: phase names describe parts of the watering day. Steering direction and watering phase describe different things, so keep both labels clear.

visual.title: Name a direction before a setting
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: The crop sees more than one setting
body: Irrigation interacts with climate and light.
Substrate, cultivar and crop stage matter.
slides.narration: Irrigation changes root-region conditions. Climate and light also affect the response. More water availability can support a vegetative direction, while greater dryback can contribute to a generative direction in suitable conditions. These are broad concepts, not instructions to increase stress. The same settings can behave differently with another medium, plant variety, crop stage or climate. Use local measurements and the responsible grower’s judgement. This lesson supplies no recipe or substrate EC target.

visual.title: The crop sees more than one setting
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: What the planner slider actually does
slides.narration: An endpoint is one set of configured values at the end of the slider. A profile holds both endpoints for reuse. The planner has a vegetative endpoint at zero and a generative endpoint at one hundred. Between them, it blends each supported setting. The operator supplies those endpoint values. The slider does not discover safe limits from the container size. Existing installations may begin with equal endpoints. In that case, moving the slider changes no effective value until endpoints differ.

visual.title: What the planner slider actually does
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Worked example: halfway between endpoints
body: Example P0 wait endpoints: 30 and 50 minutes.
The actual setting step controls rounding.
slides.narration: Use fictional P zero wait endpoints to understand the arithmetic. One endpoint is thirty minutes and the other is fifty. Their difference is twenty minutes. A slider at fifty uses half that difference: ten minutes. Add ten to thirty to obtain forty minutes. The program rounds to the step supported by the actual setting. This example illustrates blending only. It does not establish a suitable morning wait for any crop or installation.

visual.title: Worked example: halfway between endpoints
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Blend fictional endpoints of 30 and 50 minutes at slider 50.
steps: Difference: 50 - 30 = 20 minutes.
Fraction: 50 / 100 = 0.5.
Blend: 30 + 0.5 × 20 = 40 minutes, before parameter-step rounding.
workedExample.answer: 40 minutes in this arithmetic example. Endpoint suitability remains a separate local decision.

slides.title: Pause and complete the blend
slides.narration: Complete the partly filled example before reading the result. Keep the endpoints at thirty and fifty minutes. Move the slider to twenty-five. What fraction of the difference does that use? Pause now. The fraction is one quarter. One quarter of twenty is five, so the arithmetic result is thirty-five minutes before any required rounding. Now ask what happens if both endpoints are thirty. Every slider position produces thirty because their difference is zero.

visual.title: Pause and complete the blend
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Try new endpoints independently
body: Name two limits of that result.
slides.narration: Now work independently with new endpoints: twenty and sixty minutes. The slider is seventy-five. Calculate the result before you continue. Three quarters of the forty-minute difference is thirty. Add that to twenty to obtain fifty minutes. State two limits of this answer. It is arithmetic, not a recommendation. It does not predict the actual crop response. Remember that other supported endpoint settings also blend; inspect the whole profile rather than one number.

visual.title: Try new endpoints independently
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Review scope and evidence
body: Shared profiles can affect several schedule blocks.
A preview is a draft, not applied control.
slides.narration: Recall A5: an EC value needs a measurement type before comparison. Apply that discipline when reviewing endpoint EC fields. Also check units, the intended zone, and every schedule block using a shared profile. A profile edit can affect those references when the plan is applied through its workflow. Previewing a slider change is not applying a plan. Save, arm and activation are separate ideas taught later. Practise with fictional data and record the limits of your conclusion.

visual.title: Review scope and evidence
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

practice.prompt: On paper, blend fictional endpoints of 40 and 80 minutes at slider 25. Repeat with both endpoints at 40. Explain why neither calculation proves the values are suitable for a 5 L container.
hints: Use first endpoint + slider/100 × (second - first).
A zero endpoint difference gives zero change.
practice.success: 50 minutes; then 40 minutes. Pot size alone cannot establish safe timing, VWC, EC or crop response.

quiz.prompt: Both configured endpoints are 45. What happens to that parameter when the slider moves?

options.text: It always doubles.
options.feedback: The blend uses the endpoint difference. Here the difference is zero.

options.text: It stays at 45.
options.feedback: Equal endpoints give the same value at every slider position.

options.text: The program invents a crop-specific range.
options.feedback: The operator must provide suitable endpoints. The slider only blends them.

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly separates stage and bias?

options.text: Every flowering crop must use the generative endpoint.
options.feedback: Growth stage and steering direction differ. Suitable direction requires crop context and evidence.

options.text: Generative bias means a guaranteed yield increase.
options.feedback: A management direction does not guarantee yield or another crop response.

options.text: A flowering crop can receive a vegetative bias for a locally justified purpose.
options.feedback: Bias is the intended management direction; stage alone does not select a complete recipe.

quiz.prompt: What does pot size alone establish about endpoint suitability?

options.text: All safe VWC and EC settings.
options.feedback: Medium, crop, calibration, delivery and climate also matter.

options.text: It does not establish a complete safe recipe.
options.feedback: Container volume is one input. Local evidence and competent review are still required.

options.text: The exact number of daily shots.
options.feedback: Events depend on actual conditions and rules, not volume alone.

quiz.prompt: Endpoints are 20 and 60 minutes. What is the blend at slider 75 before rounding?

options.text: 50 minutes
75 minutes
options.feedback: The slider is a fraction of the endpoint difference, not a time in minutes.

options.text: 30 minutes
options.feedback: Thirty is the blended increase. Add it to the first endpoint, 20, to obtain 50.

instructions: Explain the difference between crop stage, phase and steering bias.
Calculate a fictional blend and an equal-endpoint case.
List the local crop and equipment evidence needed before real endpoints are chosen.
